tagline: Built across a dozen islands on the Oder, Wrocław has a colourful market square, a Gothic cathedral island lit by gas lamps and hundreds of tiny bronze dwarfs hidden around town.
overview: Wrocław, the historic capital of Silesia, has belonged to Bohemia, the Habsburgs, Prussia and Germany before becoming Polish in 1945. The city spreads across islands in the Oder River joined by more than 100 bridges, which gives it the nickname 'the Venice of Poland'.

Its Market Square is one of the largest in Poland, centred on the Gothic Old Town Hall and lined with pastel merchant houses. Ostrów Tumski, the oldest part of the city, is home to the twin-towered Cathedral of St John the Baptist, and its gas lamps are still lit by hand each evening.

Since 2005 hundreds of small bronze dwarfs, or krasnale, have appeared on pavements and windowsills, and hunting for them is a favourite pastime. The Centennial Hall, a UNESCO-listed early concrete dome, and the huge Racławice Panorama painting are other highlights.
